segments.translation: To make firm the meaning already stated, he has said in [verses]{pada} of [conduct]{carya}:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song as [verses]{pada} of [conduct]{carya} spoken to make firm a meaning already stated; he does not say which meaning. The Tibetan instead has “to teach the stated meaning” and “with another song” (cp.13.m1).

flags.note: caryā[padai]r: “padai” is Shastri’s restoration at the folio break; the surviving -r abhihitaṃ needs an instrumental plural, and the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has glu, “song”, so a word for the songs is secure even if its exact form is not.
taiḥ taken as the honorific plural “by him”, the poet (Kṛṣṇācārya, named in the attribution written before the song). It could instead agree with caryāpadaiḥ: “by those verses of conduct”.

the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads gsungs pa'i don bstan par bya ba'i phyir glu gzhan gyis gsungs te, “in order to teach the meaning that was stated, he spoke with another song”: bstan pa, “teach, show”, where the Sanskrit has dṛḍhīkaraṇa, “making firm”, and glu gzhan, “another song”, where it has taiś caryāpadaiḥ (as if reading anyaiḥ or aparaiḥ, or rendering freely).

segments.translit: tiśaraṇetyādi | trayaṃ kāyavākcittaṃ | yasmin caturthe śara[ṇe] līna[ṃ] gataṃ taṃ mahāsukhakāyaṃ naukā sandhyābhāṣayā boddhavyam | ata eva śūnyatākaruṇayor aikyaṃ nijadehe(hā) yuganaddharūpaṃ tena mahāsukhakāyena | aṭhakumārīti buddhaiśvaryādisukham anubhūtam |
segments.translation: “The [three refuges]{trisarana}…” and so on. The three are [body, speech and mind]{kaya-vak-citta}. The fourth refuge in which they have dissolved, that [body of great bliss]{mahasukha-kaya}, is to be understood in [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa} as the [boat]{boat}. That is why, through that [body of great bliss]{mahasukha-kaya}, the oneness of [emptiness]{sunyata} and [compassion]{karuna} in one’s own [body]{body} has the form of [coupled union]{yuganaddha}. “[Eight maidens]{eight-maidens}” means: the [bliss]{sukha} of the Buddha’s lordship and the rest is experienced.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the [three refuges]{trisarana} as body, speech and mind; the [boat]{boat}, in twilight language, as the [body of great bliss]{mahasukha-kaya}, the fourth refuge where they dissolve (in the Tibetan, the mind does). Through it emptiness and compassion are one in one’s body, as coupled union. The [eight maidens]{eight-maidens}: the experienced bliss of the Buddha’s lordship and the rest (cp.13.m2).

equations.en: the body of great bliss, the fourth refuge, in which body, speech and mind have dissolved
the bliss of the Buddha’s lordship and the rest, which is experienced

flags.note: After listing lus dang ngag dang yid, the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) goes on yid de ni bzhi pa gang la thim par gyur pa'o, “that mind is what has dissolved into the fourth”: in the Tibetan it is the mind (yid), not the triad, that dissolves, and “the fourth” (bzhi pa) has no word for “refuge”. In the Sanskrit, trayaṃ … līnaṃ gataṃ is neuter singular, which suits the triad (or cittaṃ alone, which may be how the translators took it).
śara[ṇe] and līna[ṃ] are Shastri’s restorations; the manuscript’s śara… makes śaraṇe secure, though the Tibetan does not render it.

nijadehe(hā): the edition prints the locative nijadehe with “(hā)” beside it. I translate the locative, “in one’s own body”. the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has stong pa dang snying rje dag gcig pa nyid ni rang lus te, “the oneness of emptiness and compassion is one’s own body”, as if reading a nominative nijadeha (echoing nia deha of line 1b).

taṃ mahāsukhakāyaṃ naukā … boddhavyam: an accusative object with an impersonal gerundive, a common loose construction; understood as “that body of great bliss is to be understood as the boat”. The Tibetan (de la bde ba chen po'i lus la gru'i dgongs pa'i skad du brtag par bya'o) agrees.

Munidatta (cp.13.m2) cites the song’s words as one word, aṭhakumārī, “eight maidens”, against Shastri’s division aṭhaka mārī; the Tibetan (gzhon nu ma rnam brgyad) agrees with him. He does not say whether “lordship and the rest” (buddhaiśvaryādi) amounts to eight. anubhūtam may be “is experienced” or “has been experienced”; the Tibetan has nyams su myong ba, “experiencing”.

segments.translit:
dhruvapadena caturthopāyasyānuśa[ṃ]sām āhuḥ —
tarittā ityādi | tena caturthānandopāyanaukayā bhavasamudraṃ kṛṣṇācāryeṇa tīrṇaṃ | māyāmayaṃ svapnopamaṃ ca kṛtveti | madhyaveṇikāyāṃ paramānande svādhiṣṭhānacittasya taraṅgaṃ ullolaṃ sukhaṃ bhuktaṃ mayeti ity ātmavedanaṃ na pratīkṣyate |
tathā ca nāgārjunapādāḥ apratiṣṭhānaprakāśe —
yāvān kaścit vikalpaḥ prabhavati manasi tyājyarūpo hi tāvān
yo 'sāv ānandarūpaḥ paramasukhakaraḥ so 'pi saṃkalpamātraḥ |
yo vā vairāgyabhāvas tad api tadubhayaṃ tad bhavasyāgrahetu
nirvāṇān nānyad asti kvacid api viṣaye nirvikalpātmacittāt ||
segments.note: Munidatta reads the [refrain]{dhruvapada} as praise of the fourth means: on the boat of the means of the fourth joy Kāṇha crossed the ocean of existence, making it illusory and dreamlike. The middle [braid]{veni} is [supreme joy]{paramananda}, where no awareness of self, “I have enjoyed the surging bliss of the self-blessing mind”, is looked for (cp.13.m3).

equations.en: the means of the fourth joy, on which Kṛṣṇācārya crossed the ocean of existence
the surging bliss (ullolaṃ sukhaṃ) of the self-blessing mind

citations.quoted: yāvān kaścit vikalpaḥ prabhavati manasi tyājyarūpo hi tāvān … nirvāṇān nānyad asti kvacid api viṣaye nirvikalpātmacittāt
citations.work: Apratiṣṭhānaprakāśa, named by Munidatta (cp.13.m3) and ascribed to Nāgārjunapāda (the glossary records the same verse quoted at cp.08.m2)

flags.note: tena (masculine/neuter) cannot agree with the feminine naukayā. I take it as “so, thus”; it could also go with kṛṣṇācāryeṇa (“by him, Kṛṣṇācārya”) or point back to the “fourth means” (upāya, masculine) just named. the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) attaches it to the boat: thabs kyi gru de yis, “by that boat of means”.
the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has thabs kyi gru, “the boat of means”, without “of the fourth joy”, and a present tense, sgrol ba, “crosses”, for tīrṇaṃ, “was crossed”.

For madhyaveṇikāyāṃ paramānande the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has dbus su rdzing ni lus la mchog tu dga' ba, “in the middle, the pool is supreme joy in the body”: it renders veṇī by rdzing, “pool”, as in its line 2b, makes the equation explicit with ni, and adds lus la, “in the body”, perhaps from dividing -veṇi-kāyāṃ as if it held kāya, “body”.

For taraṅgaṃ ullolaṃ sukhaṃ bhuktaṃ mayeti the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has chu rlabs ni g.yo ba dang bcas pa'i bde ba za ba'i rang bzhin zhes, “the waves are the nature of enjoying bliss that has movement”, without “by me”; for ātmavedanaṃ na pratīkṣyate it has 'dir ni rang gi tshor ba yang mi dmigs pa'o, “here even one’s own feeling is not apprehended” (mi dmigs pa, as for na upalabhyate, where the Sanskrit has pratīkṣyate, “is looked for, expected”).

ātmavedana: “awareness of oneself” (as the enjoyer) or “one’s own feeling” (the Tibetan rang gi tshor ba). I avoid “self-awareness” so as not to suggest the technical svasaṃvedana. na pratīkṣyate: “is not looked for”, or “is not waited for, not expected”. The negative is Munidatta’s (cp.13.m3); line 2b as drafted (“the waves were known”) has none, while the Tibetan line has one (chu rlabs yong mi shes).
mayeti ity: iti written twice, apparently a dittography; translated once.

Verse line 3, tad api tadubhayaṃ tad bhavasyāgrahetu, is awkward (the meter is sound): taken as “that too; the pair of them is the chief (agra) cause of existence”. The Tibetan reads the line quite differently: gang yang chags pa dang bral ba'i dngos med de yang de gnyis la de yis dngos por 'dzin pa'i phyir mya ngan 'da' bar mi 'gyur ro, “whatever non-thing is free of attachment, that too, since it grasps those two as things, does not pass into nirvāṇa”, as if reading vairāgya-abhāva and bhāva-grāha.

Verse line 4: nirvāṇān (ablative) nānyad asti … nirvikalpātmacittāt is construed as “there is no nirvāṇa other than one’s own mind free of concepts”, with kvacid api viṣaye going with nirvikalpa (“free of concepts about any object”), as the Tibetan yul nyid la rnam par mi rtog bdag sems suggests. Taken with asti instead, it would read “nowhere, in any object, is there…”.

The Tibetan version of the verse opens ji srid 'ga' zhig rnam par rtog / rab skyes yid ni spang bya ste / de srid du ni gnyis nyid phyir, which makes “the mind” what is to be abandoned and adds “because of duality”; its last line ('ga' zhig kyang ni yul nyid la / rnam par mi rtog bdag sems las) ends without a main verb.
viṣaya is rendered with the approved “sense object”; in the verse it may mean “object” or “sphere” more generally.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadena skandhapari[21ka]ṇatim āhuḥ(ha) —
pañcatathāgatetyādi | viśuddhapañcatathāgatātmakaṃ sva(sve)dehaṃ kelipātaṃ parikalpya mahāsukhanaukāṃ gṛhītvā svayam ātmānaṃ sambodhya bho kṛṣṇācāryapādāḥ māyājālavat skandhadhātvādiviṣayasamudrasya bādhāṃ kuru ||
tathā ca sūtake —
skandhaś ca dhātuś ca tathendriyāṇi
pañcaiva [pañcaiva] kṛtaprabhedāḥ |
tathāgatādhiṣṭhita eka ekaśaḥ
saṃsārakarmāṇi kuto bhavanti ||
segments.translation:
With the second [verse]{pada} he speaks of the transformation of the [aggregates]{skandha}:
“The five [tathāgatas]{tathagata}…” and so on. Having imagined his own [body]{body}, whose nature is the five purified [tathāgatas]{tathagata}, as the [oar]{keruala}, and having taken the [boat]{boat} of [great bliss]{mahasukha}, he addresses himself: “O venerable [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha}, put a stop to the [ocean]{ocean} of the [aggregates]{skandha}, the [elements]{dhatu} and the other [sense objects]{visaya}, which is like a [net of illusion]{mayajala}.”
And so in the [Sūtaka]{tx-sutaka}:
The [aggregates]{skandha}, the [elements]{dhatu} and likewise the [senses]{indriya}
are divided into five, just five each;
when each single one is blessed by a [tathāgata]{tathagata},
where can the actions of [saṃsāra]{samsara} come from?
segments.note: Munidatta says this verse speaks of the transformation of the aggregates (the Tibetan: their purification). One’s own body, whose nature is the five purified tathāgatas, is imagined as the [oar]{keruala}; taking the boat of great bliss, Kāṇha tells himself to stop the ocean of aggregates, elements and other objects, which is like a [net of illusion]{mayajala} (cp.13.m4).

equations.en: one’s own body, whose nature is the five purified tathāgatas
the aggregates, the elements and the other sense objects, like a net of illusion

citations.quoted: skandhaś ca dhātuś ca tathendriyāṇi pañcaiva [pañcaiva] kṛtaprabhedāḥ | tathāgatādhiṣṭhita eka ekaśaḥ saṃsārakarmāṇi kuto bhavanti ||
citations.work: Sūtaka (so named by Munidatta, cp.13.m4; not otherwise identified)

flags.note: the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) introduces the verse as teaching phung po yongs su dag pa, “the complete purification of the aggregates”, where the Sanskrit has skandhapariṇati, “the transformation (ripening) of the aggregates”, as if reading pariśuddhi. The manuscript word is split by the folio change (pari-/-ṇatim), but both halves survive.
āhuḥ(ha) and sva(sve)dehaṃ: the edition gives alternatives in parentheses; neither changes the sense (honorific plural or singular “he speaks”; “one’s own body”).

For kelipātaṃ parikalpya, “having imagined as the oar”, the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has mnyam par yongs su shes par bya'o, “is to be fully known as even (equal)”. mnyam is probably a scribal slip for mnyen, the Tibetan’s word for the song’s keṛuāla in line 3a (mnyen pa byas); if so, the Tibetan too had the body “known as the oar”.
kelipāta is Munidatta’s Sanskrit form for keṛuāla (cp.13.m4), not otherwise known; rendered “oar” as the glossary has it. Note that he makes one’s own body the oar and great bliss the boat.

bādhāṃ kuru: “put a stop to, obstruct”, or “cancel, sublate” (bādha is the word for one cognition overturning another, as waking overturns a dream). The Tibetan has dgag par gyis shig, “stop it”. Where the song has bāhaa, “row”, Munidatta’s paraphrase (cp.13.m4) has this imperative; my guess, not his statement, is that he heard bāhaa as bādhaya, “stop” (Prakrit dh > h).

skandhadhātvādiviṣayasamudrasya taken as “the ocean of objects, the aggregates, the elements and the rest”; it could be “the ocean of the objects of the aggregates, elements and so on”. The Tibetan phung po khams la sogs pa'i yul gyi rgya mtsho is equally open. The Tibetan has sgyu ma'i dra ba ltar byas pa'i, “made like a net of illusion”.

Sūtaka verse: the repeated pañcaiva is Shastri’s restoration; the meter needs it and the Tibetan lnga nyid lnga nyid confirms it. tathāgatādhiṣṭhita eka ekaśaḥ is singular (“each single one blessed”) after plural subjects.
The Tibetan transcribes the title as sU ta ke, keeping the Sanskrit locative ending, as if the translators did not know the work; at cp.13.m5 it renders the same title mdo, “sūtra”.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena niḥsandehapratipādanāya bhāvanāviśuddhim āhuḥ —
gandhetyādi | bāhyaṃ gandharasasparśādiviṣayaṃ yathaivāsti tathaiv[ā]stu | sarvadharmasvarūpāvagamenāsmāt pratinidrāstyānarahitatayā jāgradavasthāyāṃ svapnavat pratibhāti |
tathā ca sūtake —
suptaprabuddhe tu na cārthabhedaḥ
saṃkalpayet svapnaphalābhilāṣī |
rātrindivaṃ svapnam upeti jantu[ḥ]
mahāprayatnena cireṇa siddhiḥ ||
segments.translation:
With the third [verse]{pada}, to establish it beyond doubt, he speaks of the purification of [meditation]{bhavana}:
“Smell…” and so on. The outer [sense objects]{visaya}, smell, taste, touch and the rest: just as they are, so let them be. Because one understands the [true nature]{svarupa} of all [dharmas]{dharma}, and is therefore free of [sleep]{nidra} and [torpor]{styana}, they appear in the waking state like a [dream]{svapna}.
And so in the [Sūtaka]{tx-sutaka}:
Between sleeping and waking there is no difference in the object;
one who longs for the fruit of dreams should form a resolve.
Night and day a creature passes into [dream]{svapna};
with great effort, after a long time, comes [accomplishment]{siddhi}.
segments.note: Munidatta says this verse teaches the purification of [meditation]{bhavana}. Outer objects, smell, taste, touch and the rest, are to be left as they are (the Tibetan lacks this); understanding the true nature of all things frees one from sleep and torpor, and in the waking state they appear like a [dream]{svapna} (cp.13.m5).

citations.quoted: suptaprabuddhe tu na cārthabhedaḥ saṃkalpayet svapnaphalābhilāṣī | rātrindivaṃ svapnam upeti jantu[ḥ] mahāprayatnena cireṇa siddhiḥ ||
citations.work: Sūtaka (so named by Munidatta, cp.13.m5; not otherwise identified)

flags.note: For yathaivāsti tathaivāstu, “just as it is, so let it be”, the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has yul la ji lta ba de bzhin du chos thams cad kyi ngo bo nyid khong du chud pa, “just as with the objects, so is the understanding of the nature of all things”: it lacks “let it be” and runs the clause into the next sentence.
the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has the tshom med par rtogs par bya ba'i phyir, “so that it be understood without doubt”, for niḥsandehapratipādanāya, “to establish it beyond doubt”.
tathaiv[ā]stu: the vowel sign is Shastri’s restoration; jantu[ḥ] likewise.

pratinidrāstyāna is unusual: nidrā, “sleep”, with the prefix prati-, beside styāna, “torpor” (which normally pairs with middha, “drowsiness”). the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has so sor gnyid dang rmugs pa, rendering prati- literally as so sor, “each, severally”. Translated simply “sleep and torpor”.

The subject of pratibhāti, “appears”, is unstated; taken as the outer objects (bāhyaṃ … viṣayaṃ, a collective singular). The one who understands and is free of sleep is the practitioner, also unstated.

Sūtaka verse line 2, saṃkalpayet svapnaphalābhilāṣī, has no object: “should form a resolve (to dream)”, or, with line 1, “only one who longs for the fruit of dreams would imagine (a difference)”. The Tibetan rmi lam 'bras bu mngon 'dod yang dag rtog byed pa, “one who desires the dream’s fruit and conceives”, does not decide it.
The Tibetan names the source mdo las kyang, “from the sūtra too”, where at cp.13.m4 it transcribes sU ta ke; and it ends the verse with a verb, bsgrub, “accomplish”, for the noun siddhiḥ.

segments.translit:
caturthapadena mārgasyānuśaṃsām āhuḥ —
cia ityādi | sarvākāravaropetaśūnyatānaumārge [22] cittakarṇadhāraṃ samāropya tatprasaṅgena kṛṣṇācāryacaraṇāḥ mahāsukhacakradvīpaṃ gatāḥ | 13 ||
segments.translation:
With the fourth [verse]{pada} he speaks in [praise]{anusamsa} of the [path]{marga}:
“The [mind]{citta}…” and so on. Having set the [mind]{citta} as [helmsman]{helmsman} on the [boat]{boat}-[path]{marga} of [emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects]{sarvakaravaropeta}, and in its company, the venerable [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha} went to the island of the [wheel of great bliss]{mahasukha-cakra}.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the last verse as praise of the [path]{marga}. He renders the song’s [māṅga]{manga} as the boat-path of emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects: setting the mind on it as [helmsman]{helmsman}, and in its company, Kāṇha went to the island of the [wheel of great bliss]{mahasukha-cakra} (cp.13.m6).

equations.en: the boat-path of emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects, on which the mind is set as helmsman

flags.note: The equation for māṅga is a word-for-word rendering (suṇata māṅge → śūnyatānaumārge), not an “iti” gloss; as in song 8 he gives mārga, “path”, for māṅga, here as “boat-path”.

tatprasaṅgena: “in its company”, “in connection with that”, or simply “thereby”; “its” may be the mind-helmsman or the boat-path. the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has dang 'grogs te, “accompanying”, which supports “company”; the word may pick up the song’s sāṅge, “with”, in line 5b, where Kāṇha sets out with great bliss as companion, while Munidatta has him go to the island of the wheel of great bliss (cp.13.m6).

For cittakarṇadhāraṃ samāropya, “having set the mind aboard as helmsman”, the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has sems gdos pa 'dzin par yang dag par bskyed pa, “properly generating the mind as helmsman”.

For mahāsukhacakradvīpaṃ gatāḥ, “went to the island of the wheel of great bliss”, the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has bde ba chen po'i gling dang mtshungs par 'gro bar byed do, “goes as to (or: to the like of) the island of great bliss”: no “wheel”, an added mtshungs par, “alike”, and a present tense.
The closing “13” is the song number that ends each comment in the manuscript; it is not translated. [22] is a folio number.

questions: Line 2b: Munidatta’s gloss of the refrain ends in a negative (the awareness “I have enjoyed the wave…” is not looked for, cp.13.m3), and the Tibetan line has chu rlabs yong mi shes, “the waves’ coming is not known”. The draft has “the waves were known”. Should muniā be reconsidered, or at least flagged, in the line?

Line 4a: Munidatta’s paraphrase names smell, taste and touch (gandharasasparśa, cp.13.m5), and the Tibetan line has dri reg ro, “smell, touch, taste”. The draft “Smell and touch” may drop a rasa hidden in parasara (parasa + rasa?). Worth checking against the line’s translit.

Line 3b: where the song has bāhaa, “row”, Munidatta has bādhāṃ kuru, “put a stop to” (cp.13.m4), and makes one’s own body the oar and great bliss the boat. Possibly he heard bāhaa as bādhaya, “stop”. The draft line need not change, but a note on the line might mention it.

Glossary, boat: its reading “the body of great bliss … (per Munidatta, cp.13.m2, cp.13.m4)” is right for cp.13.m2, but cp.13.m4 has “the boat of great bliss” (mahāsukhanaukā), and there it is the body that is the oar. I have added equations for m4 (boat = great bliss; oar = one’s own body). Consider dropping cp.13.m4 from that reading.

Several equations here (boat, trisarana, eight-maidens, veni, wave) overlap readings already in the glossary for these segments, but in different wording, so accepting them will add near-duplicate readings. Keep whichever wording you prefer.

I have kept Munidatta’s own name for the poet, Kṛṣṇācārya (cp.13.m3, cp.13.m4, cp.13.m6), linked to p-kanha, in the translations, and used Kāṇha in the notes, to match the song. Should the commentary also read Kāṇha?
ātmavedana (cp.13.m3) is rendered “awareness of self” so as not to collide with svasaṃvedana, “self-awareness”. Acceptable, or should it be linked/distinguished in the glossary?
viṣaya in the Nāgārjuna verse (cp.13.m3) is given the approved “sense object”, though “object” or “sphere” may suit the verse better.
